newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain could need a mini-budget this year - study.
newsitem.headline: Spain could need a mini-budget this year - study.

text.p: Spain may need a mini-budget this year to meet its target of keeping the central government deficit to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product, private research group Eriste said in its monthly report.
Though it is too early to establish a trend, January central government deficit data showed official estimates are overly optimistic on both expenditures and revenues, Eriste said.
"Value added tax receipts were significantly lower than expected..and also expenditures were higher than initially targeted," Eriste wrote.
"Every forecast of 1997 expenditures shows the state cannot meet its target of 2.5 percent of GDP," they added.
The report concluded a mini-budget would most likely cut expenditure rather than raise taxes.
A week ago, Spanish Budget Secretary Jose Folgado said there was no need for a mini-budget later this year.
The budget foresees non-financial revenues of 16.1 trillion pesetas, compared to 14.6 trillion in 1996. Expenditures are seen at 18.1 trillion compared with 18.3 trillion in 1996.
Spain's January central state deficit on a national account basis rose a provisional 399.5 billion pesetas, 40.3 percent higher than the same period a year ago.
January's cash basis deficit rose to 376.5 billion pesetas, up from 151.9 billion in January 1996.
Eriste said they expect the deficit to overshoot the public target of 2.008 trillion pesetas, or 2.6 percent of GDP and forecast it at 2.394 trillion pesetas, or 3.1 percent.
Eriste expects Spain's deficit to stay around 305 billion pesetas in February and increase to 1,104 billion in March.
